title: The Evidence Behind Panchakarma Isn't What I Expected
description:
In this video, we delve into the world of Ayurveda by examining the textbooks used to train Ayurvedic doctors, specifically those following the BAMS curriculum as outlined by the NCISM. The journey through these Ayurveda textbooks reveals a concerning blend of traditional practices and pseudoscience, with concepts like Panchakarma, Ama, and the three Doshas being presented as medical fact without robust scientific evidence. As we turn each page, it becomes increasingly clear that the line between alternative medicine and evidence-based medicine is often blurred in Ayurvedic medical colleges. This raises important questions about the role of critical thinking and skepticism in medical education, particularly when it comes to health claims made by practitioners of Indian medicine. By exploring the intersection of Ayurvedic medicine and science, this documentary aims to promote a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and limitations of Ayurveda, encouraging viewers to approach such practices with a discerning eye. The analysis of Ayurveda textbooks and the principles of Daiva Karma and medical treatment according to Ayurveda principles underscores the need for a rigorous, evidence-based approach to medical practice. Join us as we navigate the complex and often controversial world of Ayurvedic medicine, seeking to shed light on the practices and principles that underpin this ancient system of healthcare.

In the next episode, we'll move beyond theory and examine the actual scientific evidence behind Panchakarma.

transcript: There is something deeply attractive about the idea of purification. Across cultures and across centuries, human beings have imagined that illness begins long before the first symptom appears. According to this way of thinking, disease is not an isolated event, but the final stage of a much longer process. One in which harmful substances slowly accumulate within the body until health is gradually replaced by disease. If those substances could somehow be removed before permanent damage occurred, perhaps illness itself could be prevented. Few medical traditions have developed that idea as extensively as Ayurveda. Within Ayurveda, one branch of treatment occupies a position unlike any other. Known as Panchakarma, it is presented not simply as a therapy for disease, but as a comprehensive system of internal purification. Its stated purpose is to remove the underlying causes of illness rather than merely relieving symptoms, allowing the body to regain what Ayurvedic literature describes as [music] its natural state of balance. Today, Panchakarma is no longer confined to ancient manuscripts or traditional healing centers. It is taught in medical colleges, practiced in hospitals, promoted by wellness resorts, and increasingly offered to patients around the world as a natural approach to restoring health. Every year, thousands of people voluntarily undergo procedures that include therapeutic vomiting, purgation, medicated enemas, nasal administration of herbal preparations, and a range of oil-based therapies. They believe that these treatments cleanse the body of disease-causing toxins and help prevent future illness. These are not modest claims. If they are correct, Panchakarma represents one of the most significant therapeutic discoveries in the history of medicine. A treatment capable of removing the underlying causes of disease would not simply transform Ayurveda, it would transform medicine itself. History reminds us, however, that medicine has never advanced by accepting remarkable claims simply because they were sincerely believed, nor by dismissing them simply because they appeared unfamiliar. Throughout history, every medical idea, regardless of where it originated, has ultimately been judged in the same way. It has been compared with observation, tested against evidence, and revised whenever that evidence demanded it. That is the spirit in which this documentary has been made. Traditions deserve to be understood on their own terms, and many traditional practices have inspired valuable modern medical research. But, once a tradition makes claims about diagnosing, preventing, or treating diseases, those claims enter the domain of medicine, where they must stand or fall on the strength of the evidence available. Rather than relying on advertisements, promotional material, or the opinions of either supporters or critics, I will begin where every future Ayurvedic physician begins, with the textbooks. The two books examined in this documentary are not obscure publications written for enthusiasts or alternative health practitioners. One has been prepared according to the syllabus prescribed by the National Commission for Indian System of Medicine, the statutory body responsible for regulating Ayurvedic medical education in India. The other has long served as a standard reference for students studying Panchakarma. Together, they form part of the educational foundation for thousands of students pursuing the Bachelor of Ayurvedic Medicine and Surgery degree. A medical textbook occupies a unique position in education. It is not intended to persuade or inspire. Its purpose is to describe what future practitioners are expected to understand before they begin treating patients. The information it contains, therefore, carries a responsibility that extends far beyond the classroom. What students learn from these pages eventually influences the advice they offer, the treatments they recommend, and ultimately, the decisions made by the people who place their trust in them. As I began reading these books, one impression emerged almost immediately. Panchakarma is not presented as a collection of traditional practices whose benefits remain uncertain. It is described with the confidence usually reserved for established medical knowledge. The opening chapters attribute to it an impressive range of therapeutic effects, including the restoration of physiological balance, rejuvenation of body tissues, enhancements of the effectiveness of medicines, prevention of disease, and the elimination of harmful toxins from the body. The books even recommend that healthy individuals undergo Panchakarma at regular seasonal intervals as a means of preserving health and preventing future illnesses. Taken together, these statements present Panchakarma as something far more ambitious than a complimentary therapy. For many people, these recommendations are not merely theoretical. Like in Kerala, during the Malayalam month of Karkidakam, which is ongoing right now, Panchakarma centers experience a seasonal surge in patients. This month has long been associated with declining health and reduced vitality, a belief that has deep historical roots. Traditionally, Karkidakam coincided with the peak of the monsoon when food was often scarce, infectious diseases were more common, and daily life became considerably more difficult. Under such conditions, it is hardly surprising that the month acquired a reputation as a period of physical vulnerability. Today, however, the historical circumstances that gave rise to that belief have changed. Modern sanitation, nutrition, and health care have transformed the way people live through the monsoon. Yet, the recommendation remains. Many Ayurvedic practitioners continue to advise healthy individuals to undergo Panchakarma during the season as a preventive measure, which brings us back to the same question. What evidence shows that healthy people benefit from doing so? And then, it naturally invites further questions. What are these toxins that Panchakarma are said to remove? How are they produced? Can they be identified and measured? And perhaps, most importantly, what evidence demonstrates that they are actually eliminated by these procedures? The answers offered by the textbooks do not begin with Panchakarma itself. They begin with a much older question. Why do human beings fall sick in the first place? Every system of medicine begins by asking the same question. Why does disease occur? The answer to that question determines everything that follows. If a disease is believed to arise from invading microorganisms, the logical treatment is to eliminate those microorganisms. If it results from nutritional deficiency, treatment aims to replace what is missing. Every therapy reflects the theory on which it is built. Ayurveda approaches this question through an entirely different framework. According to these textbooks, health depends upon the harmonious interaction of three fundamental principles known as Vata, Pitta, and Kapha. Rather than referring to individual organs or identifiable chemicals, these principles are described as regulatory forces responsible for maintaining the normal functioning of the body. Disease begins when this balance is disturbed, allowing one or more of these doshas to become aggravated and disrupt the body's natural state. The books describe several factors capable of disturbing this balance. Diet, lifestyle, seasonal changes, and emotional states are all set to influence the doshas. As the discussion continues, however, the textbooks move beyond these familiar ideas and introduce explanations that belong exclusively to the Ayurvedic worldview. Among them is the concept of Daiva Karma, the accumulated consequences of actions performed in a previous birth. According to the text, illnesses whose causes cannot be adequately explained by events in the present life may arise from actions committed before one's current existence. Whether one accepts the philosophical idea of reincarnation is a personal matter. The difficulty arises when such a concept is presented within [music] a medical explanation of disease. Medicine depends upon explanations that can be examined, challenged, and if necessary, rejected when evidence fails to support them. If a disease is attributed to events that cannot be observed, measured, or independently verified, an obvious problem emerges. By what method could such an explanation ever be confirmed? Equally important, what evidence could ever demonstrate that it was mistaken? The textbooks return to this theme while explaining why diseases sometimes recur after treatment. Their explanation is illustrated through an image of a tree whose roots remain alive beneath the soil. As an analogy, it is memorable. Whether the same process actually occurs within the human body is a different question altogether. If disease develops because harmful influences accumulate within the body and disturb its natural balance, then the obvious solution is to remove them. The textbooks describe Panchakarma as a systemic process through which unwanted substances are mobilized from different parts of the body and expelled through carefully chosen routes. Depending upon the nature of the imbalance, treatment may involve therapeutic vomiting, purgation, medicated enemas, nasal administration of medicines, or in certain circumstances, bloodletting. Each procedure is presented as targeting specific doshas and restoring normal physiological function. Underlying all of these treatments is another concept that appears repeatedly throughout the books. Although often translated simply as toxins, ama is described in more complex terms than that translation suggests. It is presented as an incompletely processed substance produced by impaired digestion capable of circulating through the body, obstructing physiological processes, and contributing to disease. Panchakarma, according to the textbooks, removes this accumulated ama before it can produce illness. At first glance, this seems entirely plausible. Modern medicine also recognizes that harmful substances can accumulate within the body. Heavy metals such as lead and mercury, abnormal metabolic products produced by certain diseases, and environmental toxins can all damage human health. The difference is that such substances can be identified, measured, and monitored objectively. Their presence can be confirmed in blood, urine, or tissue using objective laboratory methods. Ama occupies a very different position. The textbooks describe its behavior and effects in considerable detail, yet never identify it as a measurable biological substance. No chemical composition is proposed, no laboratory markers described, and no objective method is offered by which its presence can be confirmed independently. Before any treatment can be shown to remove something from the body, the thing being removed must first be identified in a way that allows its presence to be measured. Without that first step, evaluating the effectiveness of the treatment becomes extraordinarily difficult. But, ama is only the foundation. The textbooks go much further. They do not merely claim that panchakarma removes ama. They claim that it prevents disease, restores health, rejuvenates the body, and treats an astonishing range of medical conditions. Those are extraordinary claims. And extraordinary medical claims require extraordinarily good evidence. In the next part of this investigation, I will leave theory behind and examine evidence itself. What do clinical trials actually show? Do the studies support the confidence with which these textbooks present panchakarma, or is there a gap between what students are taught and what the evidence demonstrates? That is where the real investigation begins. If you'd like me to continue this investigation through the Panchakarma textbooks, analyzing their claims >> [music] >> one by one and comparing them with the best available scientific evidence, then please let me know. Like and hype this video. Share it with someone who believes these claims. And most importantly, leave a comment. The more people this video reaches, the more worthwhile it becomes for me to continue this series because we are only getting started.
